books.section: Topic 4.3 Politics and Regional Interests, C. A Temporary Truce on the Slavery Question in the Pre-Civil War Period

stimulus.text: A Republican campaign broadside map of the United States, published in 1856, colors free states and slave states differently and draws a line across the western territories labeled as the Missouri Compromise line. The territories beyond the line are marked as lands “whose destiny is yet to be decided.”
stimulus.source_note: Map of the United States, showing by colors the area of freedom and slavery, published by G. W. Elliott, New York, 1856 (Republican campaign broadside; scan of pre-1930 original). Public domain.

source: original; stimulus is an 1856 Republican campaign broadside map showing the Missouri Compromise line (public domain, in the shared image pool as 5s24-ch14-mcq-01)
stem: The mapmaker colors Missouri as a slave state even though it lies north of the compromise line because

options.text: Missouri had voted to ban slavery when it joined the Union in 1821
options.misconception: Missouri entered as a slave state; a ban reverses the Compromise.

options.text: the line applied only to states, not to territories
options.misconception: The line applied to the remaining Louisiana territory; Missouri was the exception written into the law.

options.text: the mapmaker made an error in coloring the map
options.misconception: The coloring follows the law; Missouri slave and Maine free was the bargain itself.

options.text: the Compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state, the exception to its own line

rationales.A: Missouri joined the Union as a slave state in 1821. A state that banned slavery would not need a compromise to get in.
rationales.B: The 36°30′ line governed the rest of the Louisiana territory. Missouri was the one state the line did not bind, because the Compromise named it.
rationales.C: There is no error to fix. Missouri slave and Maine free was the deal, and the map colors it as the deal was made.
rationales.D: The Compromise drew the line and then made Missouri the exception to it, admitting it as a slave state north of the line. The map shows the law as written.
rationales.general:
1. Find Missouri on the map. It is colored as a slave state, north of the line.
2. Ask what the Compromise said. Missouri enters slave, Maine free, and slavery is barred north of 36°30′ elsewhere.
3. Ask how both can be true. A law can draw a rule and name its own exception.
4. Put it together. Missouri is the exception the Compromise wrote for itself.
Background: free and slave states stood eleven to eleven, so Missouri alone would have tipped the Senate.
Remember: when a rule and a case seem to clash, check whether the rule names an exception.

figures.caption: Republican campaign broadside map of 1856 showing free and slave areas and the Missouri Compromise line
figures.alt: Map of the United States with free states and slave states in different colors, a line drawn across the western territories, and western lands labeled as not yet decided
